EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
Unassuming 1972 Pontiac Ventura Hides a Nasty Surprise Under the Hood
18 photos
Photo: Mecum Auctions
Introduced in 1960 as a full-size car, the Pontiac Ventura was originally a custom trim package on the Catalina. Its success inspired Pontiac to join the personal luxury market with the Grand Prix in 1962. In 1971, Pontiac reassigned the Ventura to the compact market, where it remained through 1977.
Pontiac first joined the compact car market in 1961 with the Tempest. The latter also came with the company's very first inline-four engine. However, the brand's foray into this niche was short-lived; the Tempest became a mid-size car in 1964. While all the other Big Three divisions continued to offer compact cars, Pontiac opted out.
The story goes that GM prioritised the higher profit margins of the larger Pontiac models, leaving the cheaper compact segment to Chevrolet and its Chevy II/Nova. It was also a matter of protecting Pontiac's performance-oriented image. Instead of a traditional economy compact, Pontiac debuted the Firebird pony car as its smallest vehicle in 1967.
That changed in 1971 following the sudden collapse of the muscle car market. With the GTO no longer popular, GM gave Pontiac access to the X-body platform that had been underpinning the Chevy II/Nova since 1962 . The Ventura II was born. Additionally, both Buick and Oldsmobile introduced X-body compacts in 1973 (the Apollo and Omega, respectively).
The Ventura II was quite successful. The compact moved over 500,000 units through 1977, with record sales of 96,500 examples in 1973. Unsurprisingly given the high production numbers and low performance, the Ventura II is not a desirable classic today. However, this all-black 1972 coupe is definitely worth a closer look.
How so? Well, while it may look totally stock inside and out, this Ventura packs a beefed-up engine and a very long list of powertrain enhancements. The Poncho came standard with an inline-six in 1972, while the options list included two small-block V8 mills. The range-topping 350-cubic-inch (5.7-liter) powerplant delivered only 160 horsepower.
This Ventura was born with the latter based on the VIN, but the original V8 has been removed to make way for a nasty LSA-type unit . It's a supercharged 6.2-liter mill by Nickey Performance. There's no info on how powerful it is, but these Stage II engines delivered at least 600 horsepower.
All that oomph hits the rear wheels through a bespoke automatic transmission and a 10-bolt rear end with forged Moser axles and a Detroit locker. The list of upgrades also includes a Holley Terminator X engine management unit, an aluminium radiator with dual electric fans, and a custom cold air intake.
The Ventura also has stainless long-tube headers and mufflers, a race-spec driveshaft, adjustable shocks, front disc brakes, a CalTracs traction system, and a six-point roll bar. This Pontiac is ready to hit the drag strip and smoke any iconic muscle car from the golden era.
I found this Ventura while browsing the lots of Mecum's upcoming Las Vegas 2026 auction in November. It will cross the block on November 14, and it will probably become one of the most expensive compact Venturas ever sold at public auction.

WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 09: U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) speaks on impeaching U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth outside the U.S. Capitol on November 09, 2026 in Washington, DC. Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Secretary Hegseth over the U.S. war with Iran. (Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — In a move that will delay an impeachment vote for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, House lawmakers today opted to refer the impeachment resolution to the House Judiciary Committee for further consideration.
The motion passed on a 211 to 204 vote and concerned eight articles of impeachment introduced Monday by Kentucky Republican Rep. Thomas Massie. In a social media post today, Massie called the floor vote a “procedural motion to kill the resolution.”
In a 34-page resolution [ PDF ], Massie charged the defense secretary with committing “high crimes and misdemeanors” and called him “a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”
More specifically, the eight articles of impeachment centered on:
Three involving violations of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 related to military operations against Iran;
Alleged violations of laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, citing the US military strike on an Iranian elementary school that killed or injured more than 200 people;
Suppressing free speech through retaliation against Sen. Mark Kelly, a retired Navy captain, for appearing in a video advising service members of their duty to disobey unlawful orders;
The kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, whom the resolution describes as a sovereign foreign leader;
Conducting an “unlawful” war in Yemen; and
Extrajudicial killings tied to the strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific.
The vote effectively puts the impeachment effort on ice for the remainder of the current Congress, sending Massie’s resolution to the House Judiciary Committee rather than allowing it to advance toward a floor vote. The committee can choose to consider the articles of impeachment, but it is not obligated to take them up. Without further action, the resolution is unlikely to advance before the current Congress ends.
The referral does not permanently foreclose impeachment proceedings against Hegseth. Any effort to revive the matter when the next Congressis sworn in next year, however, would require lawmakers to introduce a new resolution and begin the process again.
Ahead of today’s vote, Hegseth held his first press conference at the Pentagon in six months and used the stage to push back against the impeachment charges by saying they stemmed from “policy disagreements.”
“What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability,” Hegseth told reporters Tuesday. “It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”
“I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow,” he later said.
The House has only impeached two cabinet secretaries: Secretary of War William Belknap in 1876 and Secretary of Homeland Security Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. (Though Hegseth refers to himself as the Secretary of War, his official title remains Secretary of Defense.) Neither was convicted by the Senate.
For now, President Donald Trump is publicly backing his sitting defense secretary, taking to social media Tuesday to write, “‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.
